prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B005 alone, Katori and Ye. The chair asks what the magic-wavelength lattice adds beyond the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. My answer in one sentence: the comb made optical frequencies countable and the ion work showed that one well-controlled quantum system can be a clock, but neither provided a way to cancel the trapping-induced light shift while holding thousands of neutral atoms motionless in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and that is Katori's idea and the reason a clock can be both accurate and fast to average. Averaging power is not a minor point. Stability scales with the square root of the atom number, so a lattice clock reaches 1e-18 statistical resolution in hours where a single ion needs weeks, and that is what turns an accuracy record into a measuring instrument. Only with that instrument can one compare clocks at millimetre height differences, resolve gravitational redshift inside one sample, and run the many-body and spin-exchange studies that Ye's group did. In short, the lattice is a conceptual advance over single-ion clocks and not only a gain in counting statistics. From my own work on rare-earth crystals I know how rare it is that a proposal is followed by independent groups at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL reaching the same performance, and that is the maturity evidence I weigh most. I do not need the SI redefinition to decide maturity, since it is a consequence of the demonstrated performance and not a condition for it.
statement.case_against: The reservation I still carry is attribution and not whether the work qualifies. Two names cannot represent Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Bloom, Derevianko and the ion-clock groups, and I have not checked Katori's 2001 to 2003 proposal against the first strontium lattice measurements in the primary papers, so the priority chronology is from memory. A second, narrower concern is that a citation which is too broad could read as rewarding precision measurement a third time. This is manageable by wording. Finally, I accept that nothing in the clock record yet shows a variation of a constant or a violation of a symmetry; the physics so far is tightened bounds plus a new measurement capability. I count that as real but quieter than a new phenomenon, and I have decided it does not outweigh the field-opening effect.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps the citation tied to precision in time and frequency and says that if the committee wants a clearly new discovery about nature, B015 or B014 would answer that better, and she lists B015 as an alternative with Zoller, Esslinger or Greiner for a third seat.
responses.response: I agree on the narrow wording and would keep the citation to the lattice clock itself, with no mention of frequency combs or metrology in general. On B015 I think we should be honest about the trade-off. It is a richer physical landscape, but a two-part prize with B005 would need three to four names for B015 alone, which breaks the three-person cap, and the allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger is the unresolved point you flag yourself. A clock that tests general relativity and constants in the laboratory is also a statement about nature, so I would not accept that B005 is the lesser discovery; the comparison is between two different kinds of result, not discovery against engineering.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether a two-part prize combining B005 with only one credited name from B035 would be acceptable, since that seems unfair to Karle and Spiering, and relies on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson to confirm that Katori and Ye are the decisive pair.
responses.response: On the pair I can confirm it from the experimental side: Katori holds the magic-wavelength proposal and the first realization, and Ye holds the sustained accuracy and stability records and the many-body extensions; I have not found any argument in round 1 for a different pair. On B035 I agree with your instinct. A configuration that pairs B005 with only Halzen would leave out the people who built and ran the detector, and picking among them from outside the collaboration is exactly where we lack information. Because the three-person cap leaves one seat beside Katori and Ye, I would not force a second part for B035 now; I would prefer to ask outside experts about the roles of Halzen, Karle and Spiering and keep B035 as the first alternative for a later year.

responses.point: Eriksson asks whether the many-atom lattice step is a real conceptual advance over single-ion clocks or mainly a gain in averaging, and says he relies partly on Lindroth, Kroll and Danielsson for that judgement.
responses.response: I would answer it as I set out above. The conceptual step is the magic wavelength, which makes the trapping potential invisible to the clock transition, so the number of atoms can be raised without paying in systematic shifts. Averaging power then follows, but it follows from the idea. A lattice clock needs different physics than an ion clock: collisional and tunnelling shifts, blackbody radiation and hyperpolarizability had to be controlled for a many-atom sample, and this was done and independently confirmed. I would not call that merely an averaging gain. I also note your doubt about method-type candidates such as B043; I share it, and for a measurement-oriented criterion I would judge the lattice clock by what it lets us observe, which is a good deal.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether waiting for the redefinition of the SI second would add maturity or only delay, and grants that the novelty objection is answerable but not settled.
responses.response: I agree that waiting would add little maturity. The redefinition is a metrological decision that depends on clock comparisons, continuity of the realization and link capacity, and so tracks the demonstrated performance rather than adding to the physics case. The fact that several independent laboratories have already reproduced the result and compared it over fibre is the experimental evidence I look for. What would change my answer is not the date of the redefinition but a primary-source finding that the priority or the accuracy claims do not hold, or a failed comparison between independent clocks at the 1e-18 level. I would also add that Mehlig's own first choice, KPZ, has a theory that is more mature than its experimental record, and that is why I could not move to it.

responses.point: Johansson asks whether a third name for the lattice-clock lineage, such as Takamoto or Ludlow, is justified, and notes that the ion-clock and neutral-atom lineages are not fully separated in the credited list.
responses.response: I considered it and I would stay with two names. The credited list does not offer a third name for this ballot, and the third seat cannot be filled by Takamoto or Ludlow without a priority argument I cannot make from the primary record: they carried out key measurements in the groups led by Katori and Ye, and the Nobel tradition of naming the idea and its decisive realization fits here. The separation from the ion lineage is clean in the physics, because the Wineland prize covers ion control and ion clocks, and a citation that names the lattice and neutral atoms avoids any repeat. I would want the citation to say so explicitly.

uncertainties: Primary-source priority: Katori's 2001 to 2003 magic-wavelength proposal against the first strontium lattice-clock measurements and parallel proposals; I have not re-checked the dates and results in the papers.
Latest accuracy and stability figures at JILA, RIKEN and PTB are from memory and should be confirmed with outside experts.
Whether the committee as a whole judges lattice clocks to differ enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I judge so, but this is a judgement that colleagues may weigh differently.
Whether a second part, preferably B015 or B035, would strengthen the prize; my view is that attribution for both is not yet clear enough to add one.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict for B005, B015 or B035. My PhD year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder is a distant link to the 2005 comb prize and does not involve Katori or Ye; I disclose it again because it bears on the novelty discussion. My WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Johansson's Chalmers home but has no bearing on these candidates, and no change since round 1.
